prompt: Design a minimal local algorithm that decides which cell of a cellular graph receives the next unit of computation budget, given per-cell potential and resistance values. The rule must use only a cell and its direct neighbors (no global view). Explain why the rule is fair and why it cannot starve a cell forever.

an engineer who wants the smallest mechanism that could work
a teacher who explains by building one small piece at a time

steps.text: The task is to design a local rule for choosing the next budget cell using only a cell and its direct neighbors, and to justify fairness and no starvation.
A purely local rule cannot find the unique global maximum in one step, so it must select local maxima, pass a token, or use randomized propagation.
Define each cell's urgency as score = potential / resistance and compare it only with direct neighbors.
A cell that is a strict local maximum can take the budget, but ties or multiple maxima need ID tie-breaking or backoff.
If receiving a budget reduces the cell's potential or raises resistance, its score drops and it stops monopolizing.
Local-max greedy alone can starve cells separated by valleys, so add a token or random walk to cross the graph.
Use a token or random walk biased by local score; the token holder receives the budget and moves to a neighbor based only on local values.
On a connected graph, the random walk visits every cell infinitely often, and score reduction after service prevents permanent starvation.

steps.text: Design a minimal local rule to choose which cell receives the next computation budget using only the current cell and its direct neighbors.
Per-cell potential and resistance can be combined into local weights, e.g. potential divided by resistance.
Use a single budget token that moves locally from the current cell to itself or a neighbor.
At each step, the token-holder chooses among itself and neighbors with probability proportional to their local weights.
A positive floor on every weight ensures all transitions have nonzero probability.
On a connected finite graph, this local token walk is an irreducible Markov chain.
Irreducibility makes every cell visited infinitely often with probability 1, so no cell starves forever and fairness is long-run proportional to weights.
A deterministic local max rule could starve cells, so randomness with positive probabilities is the minimal safeguard.

steps.text: Need design a minimal local algorithm to choose which cell gets the next computation budget using only a cell and its direct neighbors.
A natural local priority is urgency = potential / resistance: higher potential and lower resistance mean more deserving.
Use a token: the current holder compares its urgency with neighbors and moves to the highest-urgency neighbor if that neighbor beats it.
If no neighbor beats the current cell, the token stays and that cell consumes the budget, reducing its potential.
With fixed potentials/resistances, the token can get stuck at a local maximum and starve lower-urgency cells.
Add a local waiting/aging term so a cell's effective urgency rises the longer it goes unserved.
The token then eventually leaves a repeatedly served cell and reaches waiting cells, so no cell starves forever.
The rule uses only local comparisons and aging, making it minimal, fair, and starvation-free.

gaps: Global-maximum impossibility: a one-step local rule cannot compute the unique global maximum, so the design must use a token or local propagation instead of global argmax.
Explicit aging mechanism: the score must include a λa_i term, with the served cell's age reset and other ages incremented, to force eventual selection.
Tie-breaking/backoff: equal local scores or multiple local maxima need a deterministic or randomized tie-break to avoid loops.
Randomized token walk alternative: positive-floor local probabilities can make an irreducible walk that visits every cell infinitely often.
Formal no-starvation proof: show the aging term dominates bounded p/r and forces the token across every cut, or use irreducibility/recurrence.

gaps: Global-maximum impossibility: a one-step local rule cannot compute the unique global maximum, so the design must use a token or local propagation instead of global argmax.
Explicit aging mechanism: the score must include a λa_i term, with the served cell's age reset and other ages incremented, to force eventual selection.
Tie-breaking/backoff: equal local scores or multiple local maxima need a deterministic or randomized tie-break to avoid loops.
Randomized token walk alternative: positive-floor local probabilities can make an irreducible walk that visits every cell infinitely often.
Formal no-starvation proof: show the aging term dominates bounded p/r and forces the token across every cut, or use irreducibility/recurrence.
